headline: AfD wins Mecklenburg, Left takes Berlin
summary: In German state elections on 20 September the AfD topped Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Die Linke won Berlin, as Merz's CDU collapsed to a record low.
display_body: Two German state elections on Sunday 20 September dealt Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU) their worst result on record in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and left them a distant runner-up in Berlin, where the far-left Die Linke (The Left) came first. [ongoing since 2026-09-20]. According to the Infratest dimap projections cited by Euronews, in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania the far-right AfD (Alternative for Germany) topped the poll with 38.2%, narrowly ahead of the Social Democrats (SPD) on 35.5%, while the CDU crashed to 4.9% — below the 5% threshold to enter the state parliament and its worst-ever showing there. In Berlin, Die Linke led with 25.7%, followed by the CDU on 18.8%, the AfD on 16.3%, the Greens on 14.3% and the SPD on 12.1%, a result that strips the capital's outgoing CDU–SPD coalition of its majority. Merz said there was "no way to sugar-coat" the outcome, calling the Mecklenburg result "a disaster" and conceding his party had been "squeezed out" of a contest that narrowed to a duel between the SPD and the AfD. Despite finishing first in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the AfD is unlikely to enter government there, as the other parties continue to rule out coalitions with it; SPD state premier Manuela Schwesig, who led a marked comeback, is best placed to form the next administration. These were the last state votes of the year and the figures are preliminary projections, not final certified counts.
why: The results are an early verdict on Merz's months-old federal government and confirm the AfD's continued rise in Germany's east, sharpening the question of how mainstream parties hold a "firewall" against a party that now wins pluralities outright.

headline: United Russia claims record Duma win
summary: United Russia won Russia's 18-20 September State Duma election with about 57.9%, a record, in a vote observers call neither free nor fair.
display_body: Russia's ruling United Russia party won the State Duma (the lower house of parliament) election held over three days from 18 to 20 September with about 57.9% of the vote — the highest score in its history — in a contest international observers and the brief's own reporting sources describe as neither free nor fair. [ongoing since 2026-09-18]. First results reported by SRF put United Russia on roughly 355 of the 450 seats, with the Communist Party on 13.8%, the ultranationalist LDPR on 8.8%, the New People party on 7.9% and A Just Russia on 5.1% clearing the threshold; official turnout was given as above 56%, higher than in 2021. The liberal Yabloko party was initially approved and then struck from ballots, and observers reported hundreds of monitors barred from polling stations, pre-filled ballots and people registered for online voting without their consent — a system critics call opaque and open to manipulation. For the first time the vote was staged in the Russian-occupied portions of Ukraine's Luhansk, Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions and in annexed Crimea, which Ukraine and most of the world reject as illegal. The count lands as Ukrainian long-range drone strikes hit Russian territory through the voting period.
why: A record tally engineered under tight control functions less as a genuine ballot than as a show of loyalty the Kremlin can invoke to claim popular backing for the war, and extending the vote into occupied Ukraine is a bid to normalise the annexations.

headline: Iran shuts French centre in Tehran
summary: Iran closed the French Language Center in Tehran on 20 September on a prosecutor's order; France vowed to respond ahead of a UN meeting.
display_body: Iran ordered the closure of the French Language Center (CLF) in Tehran on Sunday 20 September on a prosecutor's order, and France said it would respond, days before the two countries' foreign ministers are due to meet at the UN. Iran's judiciary, via its Mizan news outlet, said the centre — affiliated with the French embassy and operating "for years under the guise of language instruction" — had been shut for "illegal acts that violated diplomatic conventions," accusing it of seeking to "identify and build networks among the country's elite figures while facilitating their departure." Paris has repeatedly rejected such claims and says it has faced a pattern of intimidation as it tries to expand contact with Iranian civil society after this year's crackdown on protests. On Friday 18 September Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi dismissed a French statement as "crocodile tears" and accused Paris of historic crimes in Algeria. Araghchi and his French counterpart are still scheduled to meet on Tuesday 22 September at the annual UN General Assembly gathering in New York.
why: The closure is the latest turn in a bitter standoff — bound up with French nationals detained in Iran and with the wider fallout from this year's war — that now shadows a rare planned face-to-face between the two governments.

headline: Pakistan strikes kill three in Afghanistan
summary: Pakistani airstrikes on Kunar and Paktika early on 21 September killed three of one family, the Taliban said, threatening months of relative calm.
display_body: Pakistani airstrikes hit Afghanistan's eastern border provinces of Kunar and Paktika early on Monday 21 September, killing three members of one family and wounding four, Afghanistan's Taliban government said. Deputy government spokesperson Hamdullah Fitrat said on X that a strike at around 3:00 am in Kunar's Nurgal district "completely destroyed" a house, and that two further sites — a shop and an empty house — were hit in Paktika. Pakistan had issued no public statement on the strikes at the time of reporting. The attack follows a militant assault inside Pakistan, claimed by a group linked to the Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP, the "Pakistani Taliban"), that killed at least 31 people including 16 police officers. Islamabad accuses the Taliban of sheltering the TTP and Baloch separatists who mount cross-border attacks, a charge Kabul rejects as an internal Pakistani problem. The strikes threaten roughly three months of relative calm after February's cross-border clashes — the two neighbours' worst in years — which killed hundreds.
why: A fresh round of strikes risks reigniting open conflict between Pakistan and the Taliban government along one of South Asia's most volatile borders, with civilians bearing the immediate cost.

headline: VBS report clears spy service cyber unit
summary: A VBS administrative inquiry released 21 September found the Swiss NDB's former cyber unit sufficiently clarified, with Kaspersky questions still open.
display_body: The Federal Department of Defence (VBS) published on Monday 21 September the final report of an administrative investigation into the former cyber unit of the Federal Intelligence Service (NDB), concluding that the incidents there are "sufficiently clarified" and that earlier recommendations have largely been implemented, while questions over dealings with the Russian firm Kaspersky remain open. The inquiry, run by an independent law firm and commissioned in summer 2025 after an SRF investigation revealed the unit had shared sensitive data with private cybersecurity companies including Kaspersky, found no indication of large-scale data deletion or systematic espionage — no sign, in the VBS's framing, of a "Russia affair." It said "certain uncertainties" persist around the former cyber unit's cooperation with Kaspersky, which the Office of the Attorney General is still examining in a separate criminal probe. The NDB has introduced changes including new rules for reporting suspected misconduct, and a reorganisation of the cyber unit and the service is due to be completed by the end of 2026.
why: The report is the government's attempt to draw a line under a politically damaging affair about whether Switzerland's spy agency leaked material toward Russia — but with the prosecutor's inquiry unfinished, it stops short of fully closing the question.

headline: Switzerland halts Brazilian meat imports
summary: Switzerland has barred beef and poultry from Brazil since 3 September, following an EU ban over antibiotic-use guarantees, the BLV confirmed.
display_body: Switzerland has stopped importing beef and poultry from Brazil since 3 September, aligning with an EU ban imposed because Brazil could not give sufficient guarantees on antibiotic use in livestock, the Federal Food Safety and Veterinary Office (BLV) confirmed. EU rules bar antibiotics for growth promotion and ban so-called reserve antibiotics — those kept in reserve for human medicine — in farm animals entirely, to slow the spread of antibiotic resistance. The effect on Swiss shelves is uneven: nearly 80% of the beef eaten in Switzerland is home-produced and most imports come from Germany and Austria, so the beef impact is minimal, whereas about 40% of poultry is imported and roughly a third of that came from Brazil. The industry body Proviande calls the poultry situation manageable but does not rule out price rises.
why: It is a concrete, if modest, cost-of-living and food-safety story — a rule change made in Brussels and mirrored in Bern that could nudge up chicken prices and shows how closely Swiss import standards track the EU's.
